header.contentArea: Surgical anatomy: recurrent laryngeal nerve course, function and injury

related.why: thyroid gland relationships, nodule assessment, superior laryngeal nerve and parathyroids

brief.scenario: A verbal anatomy viva before a thyroidectomy list. No diagram is used.
brief.task: Describe the right and left recurrent laryngeal nerves, their relationships during thyroid surgery, their functions and the consequences of unilateral and bilateral injury. You have 9 minutes.

beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Saying the nerve always lies behind the inferior thyroid artery.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Start with the different origins of the right and left nerves.

grid.label: Course on each side
grid.fail: Reverses the right and left loops or cannot describe the ascent.
grid.pass: Right loops under the right subclavian artery; left loops under the aortic arch; both ascend in the tracheo-oesophageal groove.
grid.high: Adds that the left is longer and that a non-recurrent right nerve occurs with an aberrant right subclavian artery.

grid.label: Function
grid.fail: Says it supplies “most” intrinsic muscles, or includes cricothyroid.
grid.pass: All intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
grid.high: Adds sensory supply to the larynx below the vocal folds.

grid.label: Relationship and vulnerability
grid.fail: States the nerve always lies behind the inferior thyroid artery, or focuses on the inferior pole alone.
grid.pass: Variable relationship to the inferior thyroid artery; particularly at risk where it enters the larynx near Berry's ligament and the cricothyroid joint.
grid.high: Identify and preserve it; do not assume one fixed arterial relationship.

grid.label: Unilateral injury
grid.fail: Cannot describe the effect of a unilateral injury.
grid.pass: Unilateral injury causes vocal-fold dysfunction with a hoarse, weak or breathy voice.
grid.high: Adds possible aspiration and the need to assess vocal-fold mobility before and after surgery.

grid.label: Postoperative stridor: bedside evacuation (SCOOP)
grid.fail: Treats new stridor as anxiety, or waits for theatre or senior help while the airway worsens.
grid.pass: Calls for help and gives oxygen, then opens a compressing haematoma at the bedside by SCOOP, without waiting for help to arrive.
grid.high: Gives oxygen, sits the patient up, prepares for intubation; distinguishes haematoma from bilateral vocal-fold palsy.

grid.label: Protecting the nerve
grid.fail: Relies on nerve monitoring in place of identifying the nerve.
grid.pass: Identifies and preserves the nerve; intraoperative nerve monitoring may be used as an adjunct.
grid.high: Explains monitoring supports, but does not replace, visual identification.

fail.speaker: candidate

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Describe the course of the recurrent laryngeal nerves.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The right loops under the right subclavian artery and the left under the aortic arch. Both then ascend in the tracheo-oesophageal groove.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: All intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. It also gives sensory supply below the vocal folds.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The nerve has a variable relationship to the inferior thyroid artery and is particularly at risk where it enters the larynx near Berry's ligament and the cricothyroid joint.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Unilateral injury causes vocal-fold dysfunction and a hoarse, weak voice.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: After thyroidectomy the patient develops new stridor.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I call for senior surgical and anaesthetic help immediately and give oxygen. If a neck haematoma is compressing the airway, I open the wound at the bedside using SCOOP (Skin exposure, Cut sutures, Open skin, Open muscles, Pack), without waiting for help to arrive.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would identify and preserve the nerve; nerve monitoring can be used as an adjunct.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Describe the course of the recurrent laryngeal nerves.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The right loops under the right subclavian artery and the left under the aortic arch, so the left is longer. Both ascend in the tracheo-oesophageal groove. With an aberrant right subclavian artery the right nerve can be non-recurrent.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: All intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, and sensation below the vocal folds.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The nerve has a variable relationship to the inferior thyroid artery and is particularly at risk where it enters the larynx near Berry's ligament and the cricothyroid joint. Identify and preserve it; do not assume one fixed arterial relationship.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Unilateral injury gives a hoarse, breathy voice and can cause aspiration, so vocal-fold mobility should be assessed before and after surgery.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: After thyroidectomy the patient develops new stridor.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I call for help immediately, including a senior anaesthetist, give high-flow oxygen and sit her up. If a haematoma is compromising the airway, I open the wound at the bedside using SCOOP (Skin exposure, Cut sutures, Open skin, Open muscles, Pack), without waiting for help to arrive, and intubate if the airway does not improve. If the neck is flat, I consider bilateral vocal-fold palsy, which may need reintubation or a tracheostomy.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Monitoring supports, but does not replace, seeing the nerve.

failures.move: Observes new stridor, or waits for theatre instead of opening a compressing haematoma at the bedside.
failures.consequence: Airway obstruction can be fatal. This is a critical fail.

failures.move: Relies on a single fixed relationship to the inferior thyroid artery.
failures.consequence: The nerve is injured where the anatomy varies.

failures.move: Says the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid.

knowledge.fact: All intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which also carries sensation below the vocal folds.
The relationship to the inferior thyroid artery varies; the nerve is particularly at risk near Berry's ligament and the cricothyroid joint.

Haematoma compromising the airway after thyroid surgery: call for help and give oxygen head-up, then open the wound at the bedside using SCOOP (Skin exposure, Cut sutures, Open skin, Open muscles, Pack) without waiting; intubate if compromise persists.
Gland relationships, the superior laryngeal nerve and the parathyroids are covered in MB-478.

recall.think: Bilateral injury or haematoma can obstruct the airway.
recall.say: “I identify and preserve the nerve; I don't assume where it is.”
do: New stridor with haematoma: call for help, oxygen, then SCOOP at the bedside

numbers.meaning: cricothyroid is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

recall.trap: A fixed relationship to the inferior thyroid artery.
recall.finish: Assess vocal-fold mobility and escalate any new stridor immediately.

curveballs.prompt: Why can't you simply say the nerve always lies behind the inferior thyroid artery?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Because the relationship is variable: identify and preserve the nerve rather than rely on one assumed relationship.
